forward.prompt:
These are every image in one clothing SKU. Each VIEW contains an original photograph and a sheet of its SAM3 mask regions. Every mask has a UNIQUE ID beginning with R; IDs never repeat in another view.
Find every visually distinct garment that has visible pixels in an available mask in EVERY VIEW. The same garment may be shown alone, worn, from behind, as a fabric detail, or partly hidden under another layer. Use ALL views to establish identity. Do not require a small visible collar or undershirt strip to have the full garment silhouette. Match by fabric, construction, color and the context. A jacket and its undershirt remain separate garments even if the layers are sewn together. Similar colors alone are insufficient. A mask mixing different garments is not usable. Do not invent unseen pixels or new mask boundaries.
First describe which garments are present and which disappear, using the region IDs printed on the crops. Then output JSON: {"tracks":[{"garment":"description","regions":["R001", "R004", ...]}]}. This is only an output schema, not an answer. List only supplied region IDs and assign each ID to at most one track. A track must cover EVERY VIEW with at least one visible region. Extra fragments of the SAME garment in a view may share a track. Unlisted regions are removed. Keep repeated styling too, if present in every view. Do not select by the item for sale. If nothing is visibly supported everywhere, return an empty tracks list.
forward.raw:
After analyzing all views and their corresponding mask regions, we must identify garments that are visible in **every view** (i.e., appear in at least one mask region in each of the 5 views). The key is to match garments by **fabric, construction, color, and context**, not by the specific view or angle.

---

### Step-by-step Analysis:

#### View 00 (Front full-body):
- **R001**: Top portion of the dress (bodice with short sleeves)
- **R002**: Skirt portion of the dress

This suggests a **black, short-sleeved, form-fitting dress** with a cutout back (as seen in later views).

#### View 01 (Back close-up of shoulder/neck):
- **R003**: Upper back/sleeve area
- **R004**: Side/back panel
- **R005**: Side/back panel (possibly same as R004, but different crop)
- **R006**: Thin strap with metal ring — this is the **back strap** of the dress

This confirms the **back cutout** and **thin strap detail** — part of the same dress.

#### View 02 (Front full-body, holding clutch):
- **R007**: Top portion (similar to R001)
- **R008**: Skirt portion (similar to R002)

Same dress, same regions — consistent with View 00.

#### View 03 (Back full-body):
- **R009**: Skirt portion (same as R002/R008)
- **R10**: Back top with thin strap — same as R006, but full back view

This confirms the **back cutout and strap** are part of the same garment.

#### View 04 (Flat lay of dress):
- **R011**: Full dress — same black dress, short sleeves, cutout back, long skirt

This is the **same garment** shown flat.

---

### Garment Identification:

There is **one** visually distinct garment present in **every view**:

- **Black, short-sleeved, form-fitting dress with a back cutout and thin strap**.
- It appears in **all 5 views**, with different mask regions capturing different parts:
  - **R001, R007, R011** — front bodice
  - **R002, R008, R009** — skirt
  - **R003, R004, R005, R006, R010** — back and strap details

Note: R003, R004, R005 are all parts of the back of the same dress — even if they are different crops, they belong to the same garment. R006 and R010 are the same thin strap — R006 is a close-up, R010 is the full back view including the strap.

---

### Final Decision:

All regions from all views belong to **one garment** — the black dress. There are no other garments visible in every view.

---

### JSON Output:

```json
{
  "tracks": [
    {
      "garment": "Black short-sleeved form-fitting dress with back cutout and thin strap",
      "regions": [
        "R001",
        "R002",
        "R003",
        "R004",
        "R005",
        "R006",
        "R007",
        "R008",
        "R009",
        "R010",
        "R011"
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

reverse.raw:
After analyzing all views and their corresponding mask regions, we must identify garments that are visible in **every view** (i.e., appear in at least one mask region in each of the 5 views: 00, 01, 02, 03, 04).

---

### Step-by-step Analysis:

#### View 04 (Front, full-length, flat lay):
- **R001**: Full dress silhouette — black, short sleeves, round neckline, long skirt. This is the primary garment shown.

#### View 03 (Back, model wearing):
- **R002**: Back of the top — shows the open back with thin straps and a small tag.
- **R003**: Skirt portion — black, fitted, mid-calf length.

#### View 02 (Front, model wearing, holding clutch):
- **R004**: Skirt portion — same as R003.
- **R005**: Top portion — short sleeves, fitted, round neckline.

#### View 01 (Close-up, back of neck/shoulder):
- **R006**: Thin strap with metal ring — part of the back strap system.
- **R007**: Side of the top — fabric detail.
- **R008**: Side of the skirt — fabric detail.
- **R009**: Back of the top — shows the open back and shoulder seam.

#### View 00 (Front, model wearing, no clutch):
- **R010**: Skirt portion — same as R003/R004.
- **R011**: Top portion — same as R005.

---

### Garment Identification:

We are to find garments that appear in **every view**.

Let’s check which regions appear in **all 5 views**.

- **R001** (View 04 only) — ❌ Not in Views 00, 01, 02, 03.
- **R002** (View 03 only) — ❌ Not in Views 00, 01, 02, 04.
- **R003** (View 03) — appears in View 03, 02 (R004), 00 (R010) — but not in View 01 or 04. ❌
- **R004** (View 02) — appears in View 02, 00 (R010), 03 (R003) — but not in View 01 or 04. ❌
- **R005** (View 02) — appears in View 02, 00 (R011) — but not in View 01, 03, 04. ❌
- **R006** (View 01) — only in View 01. ❌
- **R007** (View 01) — only in View 01. ❌
- **R008** (View 01) — only in View 01. ❌
- **R009** (View 01) — only in View 01. ❌
- **R010** (View 00) — appears in View 00, 02 (R004), 03 (R003) — but not in View 01 or 04. ❌
- **R011** (View 00) — appears in View 00, 02 (R005) — but not in View 01, 03, 04. ❌

---

### Conclusion:

**No single garment is visible in every view.**

Even though the top and skirt are the same garment, the mask regions do not overlap across all views. For example:

- The full dress (R001) is only in View 04.
- The back top (R002) is only in View 03.
- The front top (R005, R011) is in Views 02 and 00.
- The skirt (R003, R004, R010) is in Views 03, 02, 00.
- The close-up details (R006–R009) are only in View 01.

There is **no region ID that appears in all 5 views**, and no combination of regions from different views can be confidently assigned to the same garment across all views due to lack of overlap.

Therefore, **no garment is visible in every view**.

---

### Final Output:

```json
{"tracks":[]}
```

region_comparisons.prompt:
The earlier images show ALL photographs of the SAME SKU for context. The final TWO cards are the ONLY mask regions being compared. Each card has outlined source context on the left and EXACT MASK PIXELS on the right. Identify the garment underneath those exact pixels, not other clothes elsewhere in the photographs.
Do the two exact mask regions show parts of ONE SAME visually distinct garment? Any identifiable visible part counts: fabric detail, tie, strap, collar, sleeve, hem or partly hidden strip. Full silhouettes and equal visible extents are NEVER required. Use the other photographs to link a detail to its garment. Two separate garments or layers remain DIFFERENT even if their colors match or they are sewn together. Background, mixed masks and uncertain identity must not be joined. A white shirt does not match a black skirt simply because both clothes appear elsewhere in the context photographs. Compare ONLY the two given masks; do not choose alternative regions.
Return JSON only: {"region1":"actual mask contents", "region2":"actual mask contents", "reason":"visual identity comparison", "verdict":"A"}.
Each description must be under 12 words, reason under 25 words. A means SAME garment (including a visible part); B means DIFFERENT garment/object/background; C means uncertain or mixed. The A in the schema is an example, not an answer.

explanation.region1: black dress with short sleeves and rounded neckline
explanation.region2: black dress top with short sleeves and side cutout
explanation.reason: Both masks show black dress with short sleeves; region2 includes side cutout visible in photo 36640328_00
